newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran magazine office attacked by opponents.
newsitem.headline: Iran magazine office attacked by opponents.

text.p: The office and staff of an Iranian magazine often critical of Iran's religious establishment have been attacked, the magazine's editor said on Sunday.
Five men "stormed" the magazine's office late on Saturday hitting staff and smashing up office equipment, said Reza Alijani, editor of the Persian-language monthly Iran-e Farda (Iran's Tomorrow).
He claimed the attack resulted from a recent article in Iran-e Farda that questioned the practice of obligatory Islamic religious prayers in government offices.

This story had been strongly condemned in another magazine called Shalamcheh which is the mouthpiece of Iran's Ansar-e Hizbollah (Supporters of the Party of God), a group of hardline Islamic radicals.
"We guess that the attack was organised by the Shalamcheh ...They took our article as an insult to religious beliefs," Alijani told Reuters.
"Similar incidents have happened to other publications and intellectuals...We expect (Iran President Mohammad) Khatami's government to follow these cases up to a legal conclusion."
The staff at Iran-e Farda, now in its sixth year of publication, had been able to identify one of the intruders and had passed details to the police and other state security forces, he said.

Several attacks on liberal publications and bookshops have in the past been blamed on Ansar e-Hizbollah and police have not prosecuted the group's members leading some critics to say group had the backing of powerful hardliners in the establishment.
Iran-e Farda advocates a civil society within the framework of the Islamic republic and presses for the right to criticise the government.
In its latest issue it warned conservatives not to block Khatami's proposed programme of reform, saying that his election mandate proved that people wanted change.
Khatami, a moderate Shi'ite Moslem cleric, won a landslide election victory in May on a platform of carrying out economic and social change based on the principle of the rule of law.

Khatami has pressed for an independent press and his supporters expect the government to relax strict government control over the number and types of newspapers and magazines that are allowed to be printed.
He was sworn into office on August 4 and is grappling with the country's Majlis or parliament to get a necessary vote of confidence for his 22-member cabinet nominees.
